module_title: Company Law 2013: Foundational Concepts & Corporate Personality
introduction: This foundational level introduces the concept of a 'Company' as a distinct artificial person created by law. It covers the fundamental doctrine of Separate Legal Entity, the scenarios where this veil is lifted, and the major types of companies recognized under the Companies Act, 2013.

core_concepts.title: Separate Legal Entity (The Salomon Rule)
core_concepts.description:
A company is an artificial person created by law. It has a separate legal personality distinct from its members/shareholders.
- Landmark Case: *Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd. (1897)*. Salomon sold his shoe business to a company he formed (comprising himself and his family). When the company went bankrupt, unsecured creditors claimed Salomon should pay them from his personal wealth. The House of Lords ruled NO. The company is a completely separate entity from Salomon; his personal assets are protected (Limited Liability).

core_concepts.title: Lifting the Corporate Veil
core_concepts.description:
While a company is a separate entity, people cannot use it to commit fraud. If they do, the court will 'lift/pierce the corporate veil' to see who is actually controlling the company and hold them personally liable.
- Grounds for Lifting the Veil: Tax evasion (e.g., *Sir Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit* case), fraud, determining the enemy character of a company during war (*Daimler Co. Ltd. v. Continental Tyre*), or when the company is a mere sham/cloak.

core_concepts.title: Types of Companies (Public vs. Private)
core_concepts.description:
1. Private Company (Sec 2(68)): Restricts the right to transfer shares. Limits maximum members to 200 (excluding employees). Prohibits public invitation to subscribe to shares.
2. Public Company (Sec 2(71)): A company which is not a private company. Minimum 7 members, no maximum limit. Shares are freely transferable, and it can raise capital from the public.

core_concepts.title: One Person Company (OPC) - A 2013 Innovation
core_concepts.description:
A major innovation in the 2013 Act (Section 2(62)).
- Concept: A company with only 1 person as a member. It gives a sole proprietor the advantage of 'Limited Liability' and a separate legal entity, which was previously only available to partnerships/multi-member companies.
- Requirement: The sole member MUST nominate a 'Nominee' (who will take over in case of death/incapacity). Both the member and nominee must be Indian citizens and residents.

important_entities.name: Perpetual Succession
important_entities.key_fact: Members may come and go, but the company lives on.
important_entities.significance: A company's existence is not affected by the death, insolvency, or insanity of its members. Even if all members of a company die in a plane crash, the company survives. Its property passes to the legal heirs of the members.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Is a company a citizen of India under the Constitution? **NO**. A company is a 'legal person', but it is NOT a 'citizen' under the Citizenship Act or the Constitution. It cannot claim Fundamental Rights available only to citizens (like Article 19), though it can claim rights available to all 'persons' (like Article 14 - Equality).

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: The creator is not the creature
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: No matter how many shares a person holds (even 99%), they are legally a different entity from the company itself.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Which case established the principle of Separate Legal Entity?', unconditionally select **Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd.**.
